relationship: related hostile rulers' plotting
rationale: Isaiah introduces the hostile counsel of the Aramean and Israelite rulers; the psalm depicts rulers gathering and devising opposition to the Lord and His anointed. Both expose hostile political counsel, without identifying Achaz with the psalm's anointed figure.

relationship: contrasting attempts at foreign installation of a Judean king
rationale: Isaiah reports a plan to install Tabeel's son, which the next verse declares will fail; Kings records Pharaoh Nechao actually installing Eliakim in Judah. Both concern foreign control of Judah's succession, but involve different candidates and opposite outcomes.

relationship: parallel frustration of human political counsel by God
rationale: The Lord declares that the coalition's counsel will not endure or occur; the psalm says He scatters nations' counsels and nullifies rulers' plans, whereas His own counsel remains.

relationship: later historical counterpart to Ephraim's political collapse
rationale: Isaiah announces that Ephraim's kingdom will cease from being a people; Kings recounts Assyria's capture of Samaria and deportation of Israel. The historical loss of kingdom and population corresponds, without claiming that this target establishes the stated sixty-five-year interval.

relationship: parallel dependence of understanding upon faith
rationale: Isaiah says that without believing the hearers will not understand; Hebrews says that by faith we understand the ages to have been formed by God's word. Both connect faith and understanding, though their objects are political warning and creation respectively.

relationship: related invitation and request for a confirming sign
rationale: Achaz is invited to ask for a sign from the Lord; Hezekiah later asks Isaiah for a sign of the Lord's promise and receives the returning shadow. The shared royal encounter with Isaiah and a divine sign contrasts with Achaz's following refusal.

relationship: verbal appeal to the prohibition on testing the Lord
rationale: Achaz says he will not put the Lord to the test, matching the law's prohibition on testing Him. Isaiah's following rebuke prevents treating this verbal resemblance as approval of Achaz's refusal of an expressly offered sign.

relationship: related human opposition reaching the Lord Himself
rationale: Isaiah asks why David's house troubles the Lord as well as people; Moses says the congregation's murmuring against the human leaders is against God. Both expose a divine dimension in opposition directed through God's representatives, in different historical settings.

relationship: explicit virgin-and-Emmanuel quotation applied to Jesus' birth
rationale: Matthew introduces the virgin conceiving and bearing a son named Emmanuel as a prophetic fulfillment in the birth of Jesus, reproducing Isaiah's distinctive sign and name.

relationship: same-chapter recurrence of the child's diet in the remnant's food
rationale: The child eats curds and honey; later in the same chapter the remaining people eat butter and honey because of abundant milk. The repeated dairy-and-honey diet links the child sign with the chapter's description of life in the land.

relationship: parallel description of children before knowledge of good and evil
rationale: Isaiah places the sign before the child knows good or evil, while describing his refusal of wickedness; Deuteronomy describes young children who do not yet know good or evil and will inherit the land. The developmental description corresponds without equating the separate land promises.

relationship: historical counterpart concerning the removal of one feared king
rationale: Isaiah announces the forsaking of the land feared because of two kings; Kings records Assyria capturing Damascus and killing Raasson, one of those kings. The target supports that particular ruler's removal, not both kings or the child's age chronology.

relationship: parallel Assyrian distress for Achaz's house
rationale: Isaiah announces trouble associated with the king of the Assyrians not experienced since Ephraim's removal from Judah; Chronicles describes Assour's king striking Ahaz and bringing no help despite gifts. Both turn Assyrian involvement into trouble for Judah's king.

relationship: related bee imagery for hostile military pursuit
rationale: Isaiah portrays the Assyrian force as a bee summoned by the Lord; Deuteronomy likens the Amorites' pursuit to bees. The insect image makes hostile pressure vivid in both, while the armies and events are distinct.

relationship: parallel shaving of head and beard as judgment imagery
rationale: Isaiah's great and drunken razor removes head hair and beard in an Assyrian judgment image; Ezekiel uses a sword sharper than a barber's razor to shave his head and beard for a siege sign. The target clarifies a comparable enacted judgment image without changing Isaiah's razor into a hired one.

relationship: related provision of honey and dairy produce
rationale: Isaiah links abundant milk with the remaining inhabitants' diet of butter and honey; the song in Deuteronomy remembers God's provision of honey, butter of cattle, and milk of sheep. The specific foods correspond, while the historical settings differ.

relationship: related vineyard image of cultivation becoming wasteland
rationale: Isaiah's valuable vineyard becomes fallow ground and thorn; Proverbs compares a person lacking understanding to a vineyard that becomes abandoned wasteland if left alone. The shared ruined-cultivation image does not turn Proverbs' person-as-vineyard comparison into a literal vineyard visit.

relationship: related sheep and cattle imagery in transformed land
rationale: Isaiah 7 describes sheep pasture and cattle trampling ground emerging from fallow thorn-land; Isaiah 5 describes lambs feeding in deserted places and plundered people pastured like bulls. The pastoral imagery corresponds while preserving the figurative people in 5:17.

relationship: parallel command to inscribe a prophetic message
rationale: Isaiah is told to write the approaching plunder message on a large new sheet; Habakkuk is told to write a vision clearly on a tablet, with its appointed realization in view. Both give a durable written form to an impending prophetic message.

relationship: related witnessed prophetic documentation
rationale: Isaiah is told to appoint reliable witnesses for the written sign; Jeremiah writes and seals a purchase document before witnesses and orders its preservation as part of a prophetic transaction. The documents serve different purposes, but both use witnesses to attest a tangible prophetic act.

relationship: parallel child given a divinely appointed judgment name
rationale: Isaiah's prophetess bears a son named by the Lord for approaching plunder; Hosea's wife bears a son whom the Lord names Jezreel in connection with impending judgment. Both turn a prophet's child's name into a public warning.

relationship: historical counterpart to Assyrian seizure of Damascus
rationale: Isaiah names the removal of Damascus's power before Assyria's king; Kings narrates that king's capture of Damascus, deportation, and killing of Raasson. This supports the Damascus clause without claiming proof of the child's speech-development timetable or the Samaria clause.

relationship: parallel near political judgment attached to a child's sign-name
rationale: Isaiah connects the newborn sign with impending loss for Damascus and Samaria; Hosea's naming of Jezreel is followed by the announcement that Israel's kingdom and bow will be broken in a little while. The child-sign and near political judgment correspond, while the names and threatened events differ.

relationship: related rejection expressed through water imagery
rationale: Isaiah describes rejection of quietly flowing Siloam in favor of Raasson and Romelias's son; Jeremiah depicts the people abandoning God, the spring of living water, for broken cisterns. Both expose a disastrous rejected source through water imagery; Jeremiah's explicit identification of the spring as God is not substituted into Isaiah's wording.

relationship: parallel foreign power portrayed as an overwhelming river
rationale: Isaiah identifies the strong abundant river with Assyria's king; Jeremiah portrays Egypt rising like a river to cover the land and destroy its inhabitants. The inundating military image corresponds, while the foreign powers are different.

relationship: later historical counterpart to Assyrian invasion of Judah
rationale: Isaiah describes Assyrian encampment filling Judah's breadth and removing its capable people; Kings records Sennacherib taking Judah's fortified cities under Hezekiah. This is a concrete historical counterpart to Assyrian penetration of Judah, not proof that every detail names that one campaign.

relationship: related warning to nations and rulers under God's power
rationale: Isaiah addresses nations and distant peoples whose renewed strength will still end in defeat; the psalm calls kings and judges to instruction and fear of the Lord lest His anger bring destruction. Both subordinate political strength to the Lord's authority.

relationship: parallel scattering of political counsel by the Lord
rationale: Isaiah says the Lord will scatter whatever counsel the nations devise and their word will not endure; the psalm likewise says He scatters nations' counsels and nullifies rulers' plans while His own counsel remains.

relationship: parallel confidence grounded in God being with His people
rationale: Isaiah grounds the failure of hostile counsel in God being with us; Paul asks who can stand against us if God is for us. The shared divine-presence argument supports confidence against opposition in different covenantal settings.

relationship: reuse of the command not to fear their fear
rationale: After Isaiah's difficult opening warning about what the people call hard, the verse says not to fear its fear or be troubled. First Peter repeats that latter command when addressing suffering for righteousness; it does not interpret the opening as a conspiracy saying.

relationship: related command to sanctify the Lord
rationale: Isaiah commands sanctifying the Lord Himself as one's fear; First Peter commands sanctifying Christ as Lord in the heart. The latter explicitly applies the sanctifying command to Christ while adding the heart and readiness-to-answer setting.

relationship: reuse of stumbling-stone language in a composite scriptural citation
rationale: Isaiah contrasts trusting sanctuary with encountering a stumbling stone or falling rock; Romans uses the stone of stumbling and rock of offense to explain Israel's stumbling because its pursuit was as though from works, not from faith. The citation develops the stone image without erasing Isaiah's protection for those who trust.

relationship: Christological use of the stone and differing responses
rationale: First Peter applies the stone-of-stumbling wording to disobedience toward Christ, while distinguishing the honor of believers. Isaiah likewise distinguishes those trusting the Lord from the trapped house, though its supplied wording presents sanctuary and avoidance of stumbling conditionally.

relationship: related falling and breaking in the stone context
rationale: After Isaiah's rock-and-stumbling imagery, many fall and are broken; Jesus says that everyone falling upon the rejected stone will be shattered. The shared fall-and-break consequence links the adjacent stone contexts without identifying every group or event.

relationship: parallel exposure of obstructed access to divine instruction
rationale: Isaiah announces the revealing of those sealing the law so it may not be learned; Jesus condemns law experts for taking away the key of knowledge and hindering entry. Both expose people obstructing others' access to instruction, using different images.

relationship: quotation of the declaration of trust
rationale: Hebrews quotes the declaration of trust immediately before quoting Isaiah's children saying, placing both in its argument about the Son and His brothers. The target matches Isaiah's trust clause, not the additional statement about God's hidden face.

relationship: explicit quotation of the speaker and God-given children
rationale: Hebrews repeats 'I and the children whom God gave Me' within its account of the Son's solidarity with those He sanctifies. This directly takes up Isaiah's speaker-and-children sign language in a new stated application.

relationship: parallel rejection of consulting mediums and the dead
rationale: Isaiah challenges seeking belly-speakers and the dead concerning the living instead of turning to God; Deuteronomy prohibits mediums and inquiry of the dead among practices detestable to the Lord.

relationship: narrative instance of seeking a medium instead of the Lord
rationale: Chronicles explains Saul's death by disobedience, inquiry through a spirit medium, and failure to seek the Lord. That concrete contrast corresponds to Isaiah's question why a people consults the dead instead of its God; Chronicles also expressly says Samuel answered Saul.

relationship: parallel inescapable darkness in the judgment scene
rationale: Isaiah describes affliction, confinement, and darkness preventing sight; Amos warns that the Lord's day brings darkness without brightness and escape from one danger into another. The shared oppressive darkness expresses judgment rather than relief.

relationship: explicit geographical quotation applied to Jesus in Galilee
rationale: Matthew identifies Jesus' settlement in Capernaum with Isaiah's Zebulun, Naphtali, sea-way, beyond-Jordan, and Galilee-of-the-nations language. The quotation continues into the light saying, while the geographic phrases are those supplied here in Isaiah 8:23.
